title: Climbing Stairs
summary: Count the ways to climb n steps taking 1 or 2 at a time. The last move to step i came from step i−1 or i−2, so `ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2)`. Only the last two values are needed.

complexity.note: Two rolling variables instead of an array.

intuition: Every route to step i ends with a 1-step from i−1 or a 2-step from i−2.
Those two groups don't overlap, so add them.
It's the Fibonacci sequence shifted by one.
pitfalls: Plain recursion without memoisation is O(2ⁿ).
Off-by-one in the base cases: ways(1) = 1, ways(2) = 2.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
summary: Each step has a cost to step on; you can start at step 0 or 1 and climb 1 or 2 at a time. The cheapest way to reach step i is `min(dp[i−1] + cost[i−1], dp[i−2] + cost[i−2])`. The top is one past the last step.

complexity.note: Can be reduced to O(1) with two variables.

intuition: `dp[i]` = cheapest cost to stand on step i (before paying its own cost).
`dp[0] = dp[1] = 0`: you can start on either for free.
The answer is `dp[n]`, the floor above the last step.
pitfalls: Charging the cost of the step you land on instead of the one you leave.

title: House Robber
summary: Rob houses in a row for the most money without robbing two neighbours. For each house: either skip it (keep the best so far) or rob it (its money plus the best up to two houses back). Keep two rolling values.

complexity.note: Two variables: best including up to i−1 and up to i−2.

intuition: `best(i) = max(best(i−1), best(i−2) + nums[i])`.
`prev1` is the best up to the previous house, `prev2` up to the one before.
Skipping two houses in a row is never forced; the recurrence handles it.
pitfalls: Greedy (take every other house) fails on [2, 1, 1, 2].
Initialising with nums[0] and nums[1] separately leads to edge-case bugs; zeros work.

title: House Robber II
summary: Houses are in a circle, so the first and last are neighbours. Either the first house is skipped or the last one is. Run the linear House Robber on houses 0..n−2 and on 1..n−1, and take the better result.
intuition: You can't rob both house 0 and house n−1.
So the answer is the best of the two straight-line cases that each exclude one of them.
One house is a special case: rob it.
pitfalls: Forgetting the single-house case (both ranges would be empty).
Excluding both ends at once loses answers.

title: Coin Change
summary: Find the fewest coins that make `amount`, with unlimited coins of each type. `dp[a]` is the fewest coins for amount a; for each coin c, `dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a − c] + 1)`. Fill amounts from 0 upward.

complexity.note: S = amount, k = number of coin types.

intuition: The last coin used was some c, leaving `a − c` to be made optimally.
Use `amount + 1` as infinity: no answer can need that many coins.
If `dp[amount]` is still infinity, return -1.
pitfalls: Greedy (largest coin first) fails: coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6 → greedy 4+1+1, best 3+3.
Using Integer.MAX_VALUE as infinity overflows when you add 1.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
summary: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in O(n log n). Keep `tails`, where `tails[k]` is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary-search the first tail ≥ it and replace it (or append if none).

complexity.note: One binary search per element. The O(n²) DP is the simpler alternative.

intuition: A smaller tail is always better: it leaves more room for future numbers.
`tails` stays sorted, so binary search applies.
Replacing doesn't change the length; appending extends the best length by one.
`tails` isn't an actual subsequence, but its length is the answer.
pitfalls: Using `>` instead of `>=` in the search allows equal values (non-strict LIS).
Returning `tails` as the subsequence; it isn't one.

title: Word Break
summary: Can the string be split into dictionary words? `dp[i]` is true if the first i characters can be split. `dp[i]` is true when some `dp[j]` is true and `s[j..i)` is a word.

complexity.note: n² (j, i) pairs, each with a substring lookup of length up to L.

intuition: `dp[0] = true`: the empty prefix is always splittable.
For each end i, look for a split point j where the prefix works and the rest is a word.
Limiting j to the longest word length speeds it up.
pitfalls: Plain recursion without memoisation is exponential.

title: Decode Ways
summary: Count how many ways a digit string can be decoded with A=1 … Z=26. At each position, the last letter used either one digit (1–9) or two digits (10–26). `dp[i] = (one-digit valid ? dp[i−1] : 0) + (two-digit valid ? dp[i−2] : 0)`.

complexity.note: Can be reduced to two variables.

intuition: '0' can't stand alone; it must be part of 10 or 20.
Two digits are valid only from 10 to 26.
`dp[0] = 1` (empty string has one decoding) makes the recurrence work.
pitfalls: Treating "06" as a valid two-digit code.
Forgetting that a leading '0' makes the whole string undecodable.

Python.code:
def numDecodings(s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)
    dp = [1] + [0] * n
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if s[i - 1] != '0': dp[i] += dp[i - 1]
        if i >= 2 and 10 <= int(s[i - 2:i]) <= 26: dp[i] += dp[i - 2]
    return dp[n]
